statement: On a scale, 1 key and 2 coins weigh 14 g, while 2 keys and 1 coin weigh 16 g. All keys weigh the same, and so do all coins. What does one key weigh?

choices.misconception: I found the weight of one coin instead of one key.
I found that a key and a coin weigh 10 g together and split it equally between them.
I halved 16 g, as if the two keys made up all of that weight.
I found the weight of one key and one coin together and stopped there.

hints: Try putting everything from both weighings on the scale together.
Combining both weighings gives equal numbers of keys and coins. That tells you what one key and one coin weigh together, which you can compare with one of the weighings.
Together, 3 keys and 3 coins weigh 30 g, so 1 key and 1 coin weigh 10 g.

solutions.reliable: Compare the two weighings. The second has one more key and one fewer coin, and it is 2 g heavier, so a key is 2 g heavier than a coin. In the first weighing, a key and 2 coins make 14 g: that is 3 coins and 2 g more, so 3 coins weigh 12 g and a coin is 4 g. A key is 4 + 2 = 6 g. Check: 6 + 4 + 4 = 14 and 6 + 6 + 4 = 16. The transferable idea: compare two balances to see what one swap is worth.
solutions.elegant: Put both weighings together: 3 keys and 3 coins weigh 30 g, so 1 key and 1 coin weigh 10 g. The second weighing is that pair plus one more key: 10 g + key = 16 g, so a key is 6 g. The transferable idea: combining balances can make a simpler group appear.

whyOnTest: Two balance facts with mixed objects need an idea, combining or comparing them, not just a single swap.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
